title: Move a casualty manikin onto a stretcher, keeping its head in line with its body
instruction: Move the manikin from the grey floor mat onto the blue stretcher, on its back with its head on the white head zone. Its neck is hinged: keep the head in line with the body the whole time (neck bent no more than 6 degrees), lift and lower the head and the body together, never raise its underside more than 8 cm above the table, and never hold it by the neck. Then let go of it with both grippers.
context: When a spinal injury is suspected, first-aid and EMS training teaches manual in-line stabilisation: the head, neck and trunk are moved as one unit, on a count, with one rescuer controlling the head, because letting the head drop or tip back while the body is lifted can turn an injury into paralysis. Done by emergency medical technicians and paramedics (O*NET 29-2042.00, 29-2043.00), lifeguards and nurses. The manikin's neck is a free hinge, so lifting the trunk alone lets the head drop, and lifting the head alone bends the neck back: each body needs its own gripper, and the two must rise, travel and come down together. The score is the worst neck angle over the whole move, not only where the manikin ends up. Unlike two-arm carries of a rigid tray or pot, the load is articulated and its internal joint is what is scored.
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top is the reference height. x points forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left of the midpoint between them, z up from the table top; the arm bases are at y +30.5 cm and y -30.5 cm. Three things are on the table. (1) Floor mat: a grey rubber sheet, 120 mm along x, 380 mm along y and 3 mm thick, fixed to the table, centred at x 20.0 cm, y -3.5 cm. (2) Manikin: a simplified casualty manikin (about 0.4 scale in length, narrower so that a gripper spans it) of hollow rigid plastic, skin-coloured, lying on its back on the mat along y with its head toward +y. It is two rigid bodies joined by one pin hinge. The trunk is a block 70 mm along x, 240 mm along y and 40 mm tall, 0.22 kg, centred at x 20.0 cm, y -8.5 cm (y -20.5 to +3.5 cm). The head is a block 60 mm along x, 70 mm along y and 44 mm tall, centred at x 20.0 cm, y +10.0 cm (y +6.5 to +13.5 cm), joined to the trunk by a darker neck bar 24 mm along x, 30 mm along y and 20 mm tall (y +3.5 to +6.5 cm, its centre 20 mm above the mat); head and neck bar together weigh 0.07 kg (0.29 kg in all). The hinge (the neck) runs along x through the trunk's head end at its mid-height (y +3.5 cm, 23 mm above the table) and turns the head and neck bar together up or down, freely within 40 degrees either way, with a light spring toward straight (0.02 N m per radian) and a little damping (0.005 N m s per radian); it does not twist or bend sideways. Both bodies' undersides rest on the mat, 3 mm above the table; the head and trunk do not collide with each other. Between the two bodies only the neck bar could be gripped, and it belongs to the head. All surfaces have friction 1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic. (3) Stretcher: a rigid painted board 110 mm along x, 400 mm along y and 30 mm tall, fixed to the table, centred at x 36.5 cm, y -3.5 cm (x 31.0 to 42.0 cm, y -23.5 to +16.5 cm). It is blue except for a white head zone across its full width from y +6.5 to +13.5 cm, flush with the rest of its top. Its long side faces the manikin, 5 cm beyond the mat. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: The scorer watches the whole trial, once per control step (20 Hz). It reads the manikin's two bodies and its neck angle (the hinge's angle from straight, either way) and, from the embodiment's state, each gripper's tool point (13 mm back from its finger tips), finger-tip point (between the two finger tips) and opening (0 closed, 1 fully open with the fingers 94 mm apart). 'Worst bend' is the largest neck angle since the first step. Heights are of each body's own lowest point (the head's includes its neck bar). A body is 'lifted' when its lowest point is more than 5 mm above the surface under the middle of its outline seen from above (stretcher top 30 mm, mat 3 mm, else the table). 'On the stretcher': both bodies, seen from above, lie wholly over the stretcher's top (to 1 mm), each lowest point between 3 mm below and 4 mm above that top, the trunk lies flat on its back (the face that was down at the start is down, tilted 10 degrees or less), and the head block's centre is within 25 mm of the head zone's centre (x 36.5 cm, y +10.0 cm). A gripper has 'let go' when it is open (opening 0.9 or more) and its finger-tip point is at least 30 mm from the manikin. Score 0 if at any moment, whatever happens afterwards: the worst bend exceeds 20 degrees; a body's lowest point is more than 80 mm above the table; the head or the trunk is more than 15 mm above the surface under it while the other is not lifted (not moved as one unit); a gripper's tool point is within 25 mm of the neck bar's centre along the manikin, 50 mm across it and no more than 60 mm above it while either body is lifted (held by the neck); a body's lowest point drops faster than 0.25 m/s between two control steps (fell or dropped); or a body's lowest point is more than 10 mm below the table top (off the table). Otherwise: 1.0 if it is on the stretcher, the worst bend was 6 degrees or less, the neck is within 3 degrees of straight now and both grippers have let go; 0.75 if on the stretcher with a worst bend of 10 degrees or less and the neck within 5 degrees now; 0.5 if on the stretcher with a worst bend of 15 degrees or less; 0.25 if on the stretcher with a larger worst bend, or, not on it, if both bodies were once at least 20 mm above the surfaces under them at the same time with the worst bend up to then 10 degrees or less; 0 in every other case. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. The score is read at the last step: the trial ends early once the 1.0 conditions have held with the manikin still (trunk and head under 1 cm/s, trunk turning under 0.5 rad/s, neck under 0.1 rad/s) for 1 s; otherwise it is scored as it stands at the run limit. On a step where the grippers cannot be read, the held-by-the-neck rule is not applied and 'let go' is taken as met. In a real trial, the neck angle is read from video against a printed protractor on the neck bar, heights against a millimetre scale on a card standing behind the mat and the stretcher, and the placement from a top photo at the end.
fidelity: Simplified manikin, about 0.4 scale in length but narrower: a rigid trunk and head joined by one pin hinge (flexion and extension, 40 degrees each way) with a light return spring (0.02 N m/rad) standing in for neck tissue; a real neck's side bending and rotation, limbs and spine are not modelled. Rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic) on every surface. Light (0.29 kg in all), far below a scaled body's mass. The mat and stretcher are fixed rigid slabs.
reset_notes: Lay the manikin flat on its back on the grey mat along y, trunk centred at x 20.0 cm, y -8.5 cm, head toward +y, neck straight; grippers open at the ready pose. Nothing is consumed.
